topic: resetting the boulder problems on a small community climbing wall

provenance.author: subagent-en-b
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is sorting and costing the problem list with closed task questions, base is a conversation about why beginners avoid the easy end. Grounded external referent: the hold store, introduced in turn 0 as the thing the setters emptied onto the floor and carried through the whole diagnosis (it decides what a setter reaches for, its bins are sorted by colour, it ends up a heap after every reset).

a: Here are eight new boulder problems to pair with their hold counts and sort by grade.
The grades run three and four and four at the easy end of the list.
Then come five and five and six and six with a single seven at the top.
The hold counts are nine, eleven, eight and fourteen for the first four problems.
The other four use twelve and sixteen holds and then fifteen and nineteen.
How many holds do the eight problems use between them in total?
base: We reset the main wall last weekend, and the easy end of the grid is being ignored.
Beginners walk past the low problems, cross the room and head for the steep back corner.
The low problems went on the slab, which is where we have always put them.
The setters emptied the hold store onto the floor and worked from whatever came out first.
Is the slab itself the problem, or is it the way the grid is laid out?

a: Sorted by grade the list opens with grade three on nine holds.
Then come the two grade fours, on eleven holds and on eight holds.
The two grade fives follow, on fourteen holds and on twelve holds.
The two grade sixes take sixteen and fifteen holds, and grade seven takes nineteen.
The average at grade five and below is ten point eight holds over five problems.
Does the total of one hundred four holds match the figure on the stock sheet?
base: The slab is very likely the problem, because slab climbing punishes beginners with fear rather than strength.
A new climber has no foot confidence yet, and a slab asks for exactly that.
The store is the other half of it, since it decides what a setter reaches for.
Put the easiest problems on a gentle overhang, where the hands take some of the weight.
How much gently overhanging wall do you actually have in that room at present?

a: Now group the eight problems by colour, following the same order as the grades.
The colours run red twice and then blue four times before yellow and green.
List each colour with the grades it covers and the number of problems inside it.
Give the hold count for each colour as a total rather than an average per problem.
Which colour spans the widest range of grades across the whole wall?
base: There is about four metres of wall at twenty degrees, over by the hold store.
It is the least used part of the room, mostly because nothing is ever set there.
We keep the twenty degree section for the strong regulars who ask for hard problems.
Moving beginners onto it would mean pushing those problems somewhere else entirely.
Where would the hard problems go if the gentle overhang became the beginner area?

a: Red covers grades three and four, with two problems and twenty holds in total.
Blue covers grades four, five, five and six, with four problems and fifty holds.
Yellow is one problem at grade six, and it takes fifteen holds on the wall.
Green is one problem at grade seven, and it takes nineteen holds on its own.
Which of the four colours carries the largest hold total on the wall?
base: Move the hard problems onto the training board side and the steep corner at the back.
Strong climbers will find them anywhere, but a nervous beginner will not go looking.
Keep the first four problems within three steps of the door, where people can watch.
Visibility matters more than angle for a first session, because people copy what they see.
Does the store hold enough large holds to set those four problems properly?

a: One change: the green problem is grade eight, not seven, and it now uses twenty-one holds.
Update the total hold count and the green entry, and leave the other colours alone.
Then give the new average number of holds across all eight problems on the wall.
Round that average to one decimal place, and give the range of grades present.
How many problems sit at grade five or above once that change is made?
base: We use the same holds for everything, whatever comes out of the store that day.
The store bins are sorted by colour rather than by size, which nobody has ever questioned.
So a beginner problem can end up on small crimps if that is what the bin holds.
It never seemed important, because the moves themselves were easy on the slab.
Should the easy problems have their own set of holds kept separately from the rest?

a: Green becomes grade eight with twenty-one holds, so the total rises to one hundred six.
Red, blue and yellow are unchanged at twenty, fifty and fifteen holds.
The new average is one hundred six divided by eight, which is thirteen point three.
The grade range now runs from three to eight, a span of five grades.
Does the span of five grades match the range set out for this reset?
base: Yes, keep a separate stock of large positive holds for the first three grades.
Beginners need something they can hold without gripping hard, in almost any hand position.
Sort those store bins by shape rather than colour, since shape is what the hand meets.
Colour only matters for reading the line from the floor, not for climbing the move.
Would your setters accept sorting the store by shape if you relabelled the bins?

a: Give a setting schedule for eight problems over four sessions, two problems per session.
Pair one easy problem with one hard problem in every session, using the grades above.
List each session with its two grades and the total holds needed for that session.
Order the sessions so the easiest pair comes first and the hardest pair comes last.
How many setter hours does that take with two setters and three hours per session?
base: The setters would accept it, though the store is small and the shelves are already full.
Relabelling would take an evening, and someone would have to keep it tidy afterwards.
That has never lasted more than a month with anything else we have organised there.
The store bins get emptied onto the floor during a reset and refilled in a hurry.
How do other walls stop the store falling back into a heap after every reset?

a: Session one takes grade three on nine holds and grade five on fourteen, so twenty-three.
Session two takes grade four on eleven holds and grade five on twelve, so twenty-three.
Session three takes grade four on eight holds and grade six on sixteen, so twenty-four.
Session four takes grade six on fifteen holds and grade eight on twenty-one, so thirty-six.
Two setters over four sessions of three hours each gives twenty-four setter hours.
base: The ones that hold up put the store bins on wheels and roll them to the wall.
Holds go back into the bin they came from, because the bin is right there.
A shelf across the room guarantees a heap on the floor by the second hour.
Label the bins by shape with a photograph, not a name, so sorting needs no reading.
Then one person can tidy the whole store in ten minutes at the end.

a: Convert the setter hours into cost at eighteen pounds an hour and give the total.
Then split that cost across the four sessions and give the cost per problem.
Add sixty pounds of new holds per session and give the full project cost.
Give every figure rounded to whole pounds, with no decimals anywhere in the list.
What does a single problem cost once the labour and the holds are counted together?
base: Wheeled bins would fit, and there is an old trolley in the plant room downstairs.
Photographs on the store bins is the part I like most, since half our setters are volunteers.
They come once a month and forget where everything lives between one reset and the next.
A picture would survive that gap much better than a name written on tape.
Is there anything else worth photographing while we are down there with a camera?

a: Twenty-four setter hours at eighteen pounds gives four hundred thirty-two pounds of labour.
Split across four sessions that is one hundred eight pounds a session.
Labour per problem is fifty-four pounds, since each session produces two problems.
Holds add sixty pounds a session, or two hundred forty pounds across the project.
The total is six hundred seventy-two pounds, which is eighty-four pounds per problem.
base: Photograph the wall itself before you strip it, panel by panel with the holds on.
You lose the record of every line the moment the first hold comes off.
A set of panel photographs also shows which bolt holes are wearing out.
Photograph the store shelves too, so the bins go back where they belong.
Those two habits cost nothing and settle half the arguments that come up later.
